newsitem.title: MOROCCO: EU seeking more effective role in Middle East.
newsitem.headline: EU seeking more effective role in Middle East.

text.p: The European Union is in direct contact with both the Israeli government and the Palestinians to try to help resolve the crisis in the Middle East peace process, a senior EU minister said on Monday.

Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, who is chairman of the European Union council of ministers, said he believed the 15-member EU could play "a much more effective role than we have done in the past".

He told a news conference in the Morocco's capital Rabat: "We are at this moment prepared to play the most effective role possible and at the moment (special Middle East envoy Miguel Angel) Moratinos is in direct contact with the Israeli government and the Palestinians."
Van Mierlo said he and Moroccan Prime Minister Abdellatif Filali had "touched" on the Middle East problem during talks on Monday and he would be discussing it further with King Hassan later.

The EU envoy, referring to Arab foreign ministers' threats to backtrack on normal relations and restore an old economic boycott with Israel, said: "I hope sincerely that the situation between the Arab countries and Israel will not be frozen."

The Middle East peace process plunged into crisis earlier in March when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu gave the go ahead to build a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem despite Arab objections.
Late on Monday, Arab foreign ministers recommended Arab countries end normal relations with Israel and restore the economic boycott.
Van Mierlo arrived in Morocco earlier in the day on a working visit of south Mediterranean countries ahead of a meeting of 27 foreign ministers in Malta next month.
A Dutch embassy statement said: "Mr van Mierlo will discuss general European questions and the Euro-Mediterranean conference being held in Malta next April 15 and 16...and also bilateral matters."
Morocco has signed an association agreement with the EU for a free trade zone, excluding agriculture, by the year 2010, and Algeria -- van Mierlo's next stop -- is negotiating an accord.

The Malta talks are a follow-up to the 1995 Barcelona conference at which the European Union and 12 Mediterranean countries put their signatures to a declaration on a Euro- Mediterranean Partnership creating a framework for political, economic, cultural and social ties between the countries.
The European delegation is due to visit Algeria on Tuesday, then Tunisia, Malta, Egypt and Turkey, officials said.
